provenance.verbatim_source: "physical_landmarks": "Verso of f. 100. Cinnabar running header ПОЛЇЕ: БА: БЛ:. at top. 11 red 5-line musical staves ruled with rastrum, Kyivan square notation, C-clef on 3rd line. Staves 1–3 conclude 'Бѡтиминѣ' from f. 100r ('твоя я-ви намъ да во-з-пи-емъ ти воскре-сни бж҃е по-ми-луй на[съ]'). Staves 3–9 feature monumental cinnabar rubric 'ПОЛЇЕЛЕѠС БАБИЛОНА [В] МѦСОПꙊ: И СЫРОПꙊ[СТ]НꙊЮ.', large initial 'Н' and cinnabar verse cue 'Тоу сѣдохо и плакахо' for Psalm 136 'На рецѣ вавилоньстѣꙗ...'. Staves 9–11 feature cinnabar rubric 'СТР҃А, ПО .Н҃. [ПОКАѦ]НЇА СЛА: ГЛАСЪ, И҃.' and initial 'П' for the Triodion post-Gospel hymn 'Покаѧнїа ѡтверзи ми двери жизнодавче...', continuing onto f. 101r.",

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L45–L49): ### Sunday of the Prodigal Son All according to the Typikon of the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee, here on p. 360, only at Great Vespers at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Господи воззвахъ*) there are not 7 Stichera of the Octoechos and 3 of the Triodion, but 6 of the Octoechos and 4 of the Triodion; and at Matins, to the two Psalms of the Polyeleos we join also the third: **"By the rivers of Babylon"** (*На рѣкахъ Вавилонскихъ*). Thus at Vespers and at Matins we follow also on Meatfare Sunday and Cheesefare Sunday.[^474] *Note.* In the five following days of this Week the Triodion has nothing, and therefore the sequence of the Octoechos follows; only at Compline do we omit the Canon of the Mother of God, as also on Saturday, and at Matins we read only two Kathismata. We do likewise also in Cheesefare Week, except for Wednesday and Friday.[^475]

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Sunday of the Prodigal Son

All according to the Typikon of the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee, here on p. 360, only at Great Vespers at **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Господи воззвахъ*) there are not 7 Stichera of the Octoechos and 3 of the Triodion, but 6 of the Octoechos and 4 of the Triodion; and at Matins, to the two Psalms of the Polyeleos we join also the third: **"By the rivers of Babylon"** (*На рѣкахъ Вавилонскихъ*). Thus at Vespers and at Matins we follow also on Meatfare Sunday and Cheesefare Sunday.[^474]

*Note.* In the five following days of this Week the Triodion has nothing, and therefore the sequence of the Octoechos follows; only at Compline do we omit the Canon of the Mother of God, as also on Saturday, and at Matins we read only two Kathismata. We do likewise also in Cheesefare Week, except for Wednesday and Friday.[^475]

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. In this context, Vespers chants are an important continuous link in Ukrainian sacred art, which requires

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L277–L280): ### The Beginning of the Great Fast *Note.* The Synod of Lviv grants dispensation throughout the entire holy Forty Days, except on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, for meat, under the condition of 5 **Our Father**s and 5 **Hail Mary**s (*Богородице Дѣво*) for the Laity, and Psalm 50 for the Clergy; on the other 3 days, however, for dairy products.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### The Beginning of the Great Fast

*Note.* The Synod of Lviv grants dispensation throughout the entire holy Forty Days, except on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, for meat, under the condition of 5 **Our Father**s and 5 **Hail Mary**s (*Богородице Дѣво*) for the Laity, and Psalm 50 for the Clergy; on the other 3 days, however, for dairy products.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts (Solemn Censing after Readings) as a scored Gradual / Psalmody (Tone 5). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: Byzantine-Slavic Hagiopolite & Stoudite Hymnographic Synthesis. Theological & Musical Significance: The iconic solo gradual of the Presanctified Liturgy. Demands solitary cantor and choral prostrations.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L391–L394): ### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified *Note concerning Bows.* On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified

*Note concerning Bows.*
On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.
scholarly_summaries.verbatim_source: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L391–L394): ### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified *Note concerning Bows.* On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified

*Note concerning Bows.*
On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L391–L394): ### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified *Note concerning Bows.* On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Vespers on Wednesday and Friday with the Presanctified

*Note concerning Bows.*
On Wednesday we make 3 small bows: at the Trisagion which is at the beginning; at **"Come, let us worship"**; at the **"Alleluia"** which is after the Prooemiac Psalm, and which is after each Antiphon of the Kathisma, and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**. And 3 great prostrations, according to the local custom, we make at **"The Light of Christ"**, when the Priest signs the people cruciformly with the tricerion; at the completion of the singing of **"Let my prayer be set forth"**; and after **"Now the Powers of heaven"**, when the consecrated Lamb has been taken from the Tabernacle unto the Diskos.[^531] On Fridays at Vespers and Compline we do not make prostrations, except those depicted in the Presanctified, which are: after **"Let my prayer be set forth"** 3 bows; after the Entrance of the Holy Gifts 3 bows; and at **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** 3 bows;[^532] and among us also at **"The Light of Christ"**, 3 bows.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### On Cheesefare Sunday, and on All Sundays of the Holy Forty Days at Vespers

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. In this context, Vespers chants are an important continuous link in Ukrainian sacred art, which requires

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.
